The canal behind the sugar mill was running high and brown after three days of rain. Darshan stood on the railing of the little bridge, arms out, and looked down at the others.
"Aditi, you first. You always say you swim better than me."
Aditi shook her head. "Water's too fast today."
"Scared?" Darshan laughed loudly, and two younger boys laughed with him. It felt good, every face turned up toward him. "Come on, if I jump alone it's no fun."
His hand was gripping the railing so hard that his knuckles had gone pale.
Aditi picked up her cycle. "I'm going home. You should come too."
When she rode off, the younger boys drifted after her one by one. Darshan stayed on the railing a minute longer, then climbed down slowly, and nobody was there to see how relieved he looked.

qa.q: Where was the canal that Darshan wanted to jump into?
qa.a: The canal was behind the sugar mill, running high and brown after three days of rain.

qa.q: What do Darshan's pale knuckles suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: They suggest Darshan was frightened himself; daring Aditi to go first and enjoying the laughter covered his own fear and gave him a feeling of power.

qa.q: Which choice turned the moment around, and what could Darshan try next time?
qa.a: Aditi's calm refusal and leaving gave everyone a way out; next time Darshan could admit he is unsure instead of daring others to share his risk.

qa.q: How might the younger boys have seen the dare?
qa.a: At first they laughed along with Darshan, but once Aditi left they followed her, which shows they only needed someone to make leaving feel normal.

grounding: A teenage boy dares others into a risky jump because he wants company in his own fear and enjoys feeling powerful, not because they are cowards.

Behind Block C of Sunrise Colony, where the parking light kept flickering, three older boys were passing a vape around. One of them held it out to Sangeeta.
"Just one. Don't be a baby."
"No thanks," she said. "I get dizzy on the swing, imagine this."
A couple of them snorted. "Seriously, try it."
"Seriously, no." She kept her voice light and glanced at Farhan, who was already standing up and dusting off his jeans.
"My mum's making pakoras," Farhan said. "Sangeeta, you coming?"
"Coming."
They walked off toward the lit staircase. Someone behind them muttered "boring", and then the talk moved on to cricket. On the second floor landing Sangeeta let out a long breath.
"Thanks for getting up first."
Farhan shrugged. "You'd have done it for me."

qa.q: What reason did Farhan give for leaving?
qa.a: Farhan said his mum was making pakoras.

qa.q: How can you tell Sangeeta felt more tense than she showed?
qa.a: She let out a long breath on the landing and thanked Farhan for getting up first, so her light voice was covering real nerves.

qa.q: Which parts of Sangeeta's refusal worked, and why?
qa.a: A short "no thanks", a joke about getting dizzy, and then leaving with Farhan gave the older boys nothing to argue with, so the pressure faded quickly.

qa.q: What would change if Farhan had stayed sitting down?
qa.a: Sangeeta would have been the only one saying no, which is much harder, and the older boys might have kept pushing her.

grounding: A teenage girl turns down a vape with a calm no and a joke and walks away, made easier because Farhan stands up and leaves with her.

Every Thursday a van parked outside the Rajgarh bus stand with a loudspeaker on its roof. This week it was steel knife sets.
"Last three sets! Today-only price, gone when the van goes!"
Tarun had come to catch the 5:40 bus back to his college hostel. He did not cook. The hostel mess gave him dal and rice twice a day. But the seller held up a knife that cut a tomato into paper slices, and a man near the front bought one, then another man did.
"Two sets left!"
Tarun's hand was already in his pocket. Madhav, waiting with him, said, "Where will you even keep it?" Tarun paid anyway, 600 rupees, and felt a hot thrill that he had not missed out.
The next Thursday, Madhav sent him a photo from the bus stand. Same van. Same loudspeaker. "Last three sets!"

qa.a: He could have paused on that question, noticed that he never cooks, and let the bus arrive instead of deciding while the loudspeaker was counting sets.

Monday. At the bank's loan counter, Raghav only wanted a small loan for a second-hand scooter. The officer slid over a form thick with words like "processing charge", "foreclosure" and "bundled cover". "Sign here today, sir, the rate is revised tomorrow." Raghav nodded along, pen in hand, too embarrassed to say he did not follow half of it. At the last second he said, "I'll come back," and left feeling foolish.
Wednesday. At the dining table, his flatmate Ankita helped him make a list of every word he had not understood. There were eleven. "Ask all eleven," she said. "It's your money."
Friday. Raghav went back with the list folded in his shirt pocket. He asked each question, slowly. The officer explained, and when he asked about the bundled cover it turned out to be optional. He crossed it out. The rate had not changed.

qa.q: How many words were on Raghav's list?
qa.a: There were eleven words on the list.

qa.q: Why did Raghav nod along on Monday instead of asking questions?
qa.a: Raghav felt embarrassed that he did not follow half of the jargon, so he pretended to understand while being rushed.

qa.q: Which choice on Monday made the rest possible?
qa.a: Saying "I'll come back" instead of signing gave Raghav time to list what he did not understand and return with questions.

qa.q: How does Ankita help Raghav see the loan differently?
qa.a: Ankita treats the unfamiliar words as questions he has every right to ask, reminding him it is his money rather than something to be embarrassed about.

grounding: A young man rushed to sign a loan he does not understand slows down, lists the jargon with his flatmate, and returns days later to ask.

Sit, Irfan, before you sign that insurance plan the man at your office brought. Let me tell you about my first one.
I was twenty-four, new in the accounts section. An agent came to our canteen with a thick file and a big smile. "Madam, sign today, this scheme closes Friday." He said surrender value, vesting, lock-in, and I nodded as if I knew. Everyone at the table was watching. I felt small, like the only person who didn't understand. My pen was already on the line.
Then I remembered my father saying, "Chandrika, the day you are shy to ask is the day to wait." So I said, "Leave the papers. I will read them."
He sighed and looked at his watch. Next day Mrs Pereira from audit read them with me. Half of what he had promised was not written anywhere. I never signed.
And the scheme? Still open the next month.

qa.q: What did the agent say about the scheme?
qa.a: The agent said, "Madam, sign today, this scheme closes Friday."

qa.q: What was young Chandrika feeling with her pen on the line?
qa.a: Chandrika felt small and embarrassed, nodding at words like vesting so no one would see she didn't understand.

qa.q: Which choice in the canteen was the turning point?
qa.a: Saying "Leave the papers. I will read them" instead of signing; waiting a day let her find that half the promises were not written down.

qa.q: How might the agent have seen Chandrika's request to keep the papers?
qa.a: The agent likely saw a sale slipping away; his sigh and glance at his watch show he wanted a signature before she had time to think.

grounding: A woman recalls being rushed with jargon by an insurance agent at twenty-four and choosing to wait and read, which saved her.

The target board in the back room of the phone shop in Leeds had Nadia's name in red: 14 contracts out of 30, nine days left. Her rent was due on the first.
When Noa walked in asking about a cheaper plan, Nadia smiled wide and asked about Noa's weekend, the dog in the lock-screen photo, the cracked case. She meant the warmth. She also knew it worked.
"Honestly, I'd grab this deal now. These go fast," she heard herself say. The deal ran till the end of the month. It did not go fast.
Noa laughed, then said, "Can you print me the full terms? I'll compare at home."
Something in Nadia loosened. "Of course," she said, and printed them, including the line about the price rise in year two. After Noa left, she stood looking at the board for a while.

Still, when a nervous woman in office clothes asked about joining, he walked her round the machines, told her the evening crowd was heavy, and offered the free one-week trial. He really believed the gym could help her; he had lost his own back pain there.

Later, by the lockers, Jomon said, "You're too soft. Trial people never come back."
Rafiq thought about his chart. "Some do," he said. The woman in office clothes signed up after her trial week.

The broker, Eshaan, kept checking his phone. "Three more parties are coming at four. Give the token now and it's yours."
My stomach dropped at the idea of losing it. The flat had a balcony. My old place had a wall for a view.

Disha, you want that robot chocolate because of the advert, na? Your Nani was fooled once too.
When I was nine, the radio played a song every evening about Laddu Lion toffees. Laddu Lion had adventures, and at the end all the jungle children danced with him. I thought it was a real story, like my school reader.
I saved coins for two weeks. At school I gave toffees to the girls near the water tap, sure they would dance with me. They ate the toffees and went off to skip rope.
I cried to my Papa. He sat me on the step and said, "That song was not a story, Rashmi beti. It was a shopkeeper talking in a lion's voice."

I spent most of last winter feeling like my life was a draft and everyone else's was the final copy.
Every morning I scrolled through people my age with white bedsheets, sunlit desks and planners full of neat handwriting. Under almost every post there was an ad: the lamp, the linen, the planner. By January I had bought all three. My room still looked like my room. I felt worse, like even the fix hadn't worked on me.
Then Naveen from my design class sent me two photos of his own desk: one "for posting", with warm light and one plant carefully placed, and one real, with chargers and a cold cup of tea.
"Same desk," he wrote. "Ten minutes apart."
I laughed for the first time in weeks. The planner is now half empty. The lamp is nice, honestly.
Pooja

qa.a: Pooja bought the lamp, the linen and the planner.

Workshop note, Tuesday evening session, Ward 12 Community Centre. Written by Nirmala, facilitator.
Tonight we looked at ads on phones. Shreya, one of our regular participants, offered to show how she checks a post before believing it. She opened a video of a creator praising a hair oil. First she tapped the name and found the small "paid partnership" label. Then she searched for the oil with the word "review" and read two long reviews from people who were not selling anything. One said it was fine, nothing special.
She also pointed out that the video began with a scare about hair fall. "I didn't have that worry before I watched," she said, and the room laughed. She said she still enjoys the creator's videos.
Next step: I have asked Shreya to lead the first ten minutes next week.

qa.q: What label did Shreya find when she tapped the creator's name?
qa.a: Shreya found the small "paid partnership" label.

qa.q: What does Shreya's joke about hair fall suggest she felt?
qa.a: Shreya felt amused, and a little put off, that the video had planted a worry she did not have; she sees the ad as trying to create a need rather than meet one.

qa.q: Which of Shreya's steps could others copy?
qa.a: Checking for a sponsorship label, reading reviews from people not selling anything, and asking what worry the ad is trying to create before buying.

qa.q: How might the others in the room be affected by Shreya's demonstration?
qa.a: Seeing someone like them check calmly, and still enjoy the videos, may make the steps feel normal and easy rather than suspicious or dull.

grounding: A community workshop facilitator records an adult checking sponsorship, independent reviews and the need an ad creates, while still enjoying the creator.

subtype: Asking who pays and what is left out [Response]
passage:
14 March, late
Watched Tomas's new travel video tonight. Hilltop cabin, mist, a laptop on a wooden table, him saying this laptop "changed how I work". Honestly, it was beautiful and I watched it twice.
Old me would have opened the shop page. Instead I paused and scrolled down. There it was, "sponsored by", small grey letters under the description.
Then I searched the laptop with "battery problems". Three separate forums, lots of complaints about the hinge. Middle ratings, not the five-star ones, were the useful ones.
Lalremsiami, from the other side of the sofa: "So is it good?"
Me: "The cabin is good. The laptop is paid."
Also noticed: the video never said I needed a new laptop. It just made my old one look sad next to the mist.
Still following him. Still not buying.
Chetan

qa.q: What did Chetan find written under the video's description?
qa.a: Chetan found "sponsored by" in small grey letters under the description.

qa.q: What does Chetan's line "The cabin is good. The laptop is paid." suggest about how Chetan feels?
qa.a: Chetan can enjoy the video's beauty while staying unconvinced by the product, so Chetan feels relaxed and in control rather than steered.

qa.q: Which checking step turned out most useful for Chetan?
qa.a: Searching for battery problems and reading the middle ratings showed complaints about the hinge that the video never mentioned.

qa.q: What might Lalremsiami learn from Chetan's answer?
qa.a: Lalremsiami might see that it is possible to like a creator's video and still separate it from the paid product being shown.

grounding: An adult enjoys a sponsored travel video but checks the label, independent reviews and the need it tries to create, and decides not to buy.
